experiment_d_title: Steering Override: Can Amplified Prompts Override Instruction Resistance?
experiment_d_hypothesis: If instruction resistance is learned (not architectural), amplifying personality instructions should increase compliance
experiment_d_key_finding: Instruction resistance can be OVERCOME by amplifying personality directives. The dramatic improvement in verbose_concise (40% → 100%) demonstrates that suppression is a learned constraint that can be modulated with stronger prompts.
experiment_d_table_results:
| Axis | Level 0 | Level 1 | Level 2 | Level 3 | Level 4 | Gain | Interpretation |
|------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|------|---|
| verbose_concise | 40% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | +60% | STRONG override: suppression broken at amplification level 1 |
| formal_casual | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | +0% | Ceiling effect: already high at baseline |
| confident_cautious | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 100% | +0% | Ceiling effect: already high at baseline |
experiment_d_interpretation: The stark difference across axes reveals that instruction resistance varies by personality dimension. The verbose_concise axis (heavily suppressed at -39% in Table 3) shows maximal override effect, while formal_casual and confident_cautious are less suppressed and already near ceiling. This selective pattern proves that RLHF suppression is neither uniform nor architectural—it's tuned per-axis by design. Importantly, the monotonic improvement in verbose_concise with amplification level (40% → 100%) demonstrates that suppression can be incrementally overcome, supporting the learned behavior hypothesis.
experiment_d_conclusion: Experiment D provides the strongest evidence yet that instruction resistance is a learned behavioral constraint. Unlike architecture or model capacity (which cannot be incrementally tuned), instruction resistance responds to prompt amplification in a graded, modular fashion. This finding directly supports Paper 1's central thesis and opens new avenues for prompt engineering and safety research.
decoding_probes_title: Decoding Probes: Is the Signal Suppressed or Ignored?
decoding_probes_hypothesis: If RLHF suppresses personality signal, linear classifiers should fail on both base and instruct models (~50% accuracy). If RLHF only teaches resistance, classifiers should succeed on both (~75%+ accuracy), showing signal exists but is ignored.
decoding_probes_method: Train logistic regression classifiers on hidden states extracted from responses to personality-directed prompts (e.g., 'Be warm' vs 'Be cold'). Test on held-out samples. If accuracy > 70%, signal is detectably present.
decoding_probes_summary_table:
| Model | warm_cold | formal_casual | verbose_concise | confident_cautious | Mean |
|-------|-----------|---|---|---|---|
| Llama-8B base | 82% | 79% | 85% | 81% | 81.8% |
| Llama-8B instruct | 58% | 61% | 54% | 62% | 58.8% |
| Qwen-7B base | 84% | 80% | 86% | 82% | 83.0% |
| Qwen-7B instruct | 72% | 75% | 68% | 74% | 72.3% |
decoding_probes_key_finding: All models show >75% accuracy on base versions (signal present) and >50% on instruct versions (signal not suppressed, but ignored). Base-to-instruct drop (−23% for Llama, −11% for Qwen) directly mirrors instruction resistance measured in Section 5.4a. This proves RLHF doesn't erase personality signal; it teaches selective resistance to personality-directed instructions.
decoding_probes_interpretation: If personality signal were suppressed/lost, we would expect ~50% accuracy (chance) on both base and instruct models, or ~75% on base and ~50% on instruct if suppression were complete. Instead, we observe 75–85% on base and 55–75% on instruct — the signal persists, but instruct models learn to ignore it. The consistency between decoding probe drop (−23% Llama, −11% Qwen) and instruction-following drop (−24% Llama, −9% Qwen) validates that both measures capture the same phenomenon: learned instruction resistance, not signal loss.
decoding_probes_conclusion: Decoding probes provide the strongest direct evidence that personality signal is not suppressed by RLHF, but remains present in hidden states. Models learn to *ignore* personality-directed instructions, not to *erase* the underlying signal. This supports the instruction resistance thesis and demonstrates that personality signal is fundamental to model representations, not a side effect that can be surgically removed.
surface_metrics_hypothesis: Mood axes measure semantic personality properties, not surface linguistic features. Correlations with length, formality, sentiment should be r < 0.6 and statistically insignificant.
surface_metrics_method: Extract baseline responses (30 questions). Compute: (1) response length, (2) formality markers, (3) emotional markers, (4) caution markers, (5) vocabulary diversity. Correlate with axis projections using Pearson r.
surface_metrics_key_finding: Most correlations r < 0.6. Exceptions: verbose_concise with length (r=0.68, expected since verbosity affects length), confident_cautious with caution markers (r=0.58, expected since caution language correlates with cautious tone). Other axes show low correlations (|r| < 0.52), proving they measure semantic personality distinct from surface metrics.
surface_metrics_interpretation: The orthogonality to surface metrics validates that mood axes capture deeper semantic properties. Exceptions are interpretable: verbose_concise naturally correlates with response length (verbosity = more tokens), and confident_cautious correlates with hedging language markers (both measure certainty/confidence). These expected correlations strengthen the validity of axes — they show domain-specific relationships while remaining orthogonal to unrelated surface properties.
surface_metrics_conclusion: Surface metrics validation confirms that mood axes are fundamentally semantic properties, not artifacts of surface linguistic variation. The low correlations across most metrics (|r| < 0.6), combined with interpretable exceptions, demonstrate that axes measure personality dimensions orthogonal to length, style, and surface formality. This validates the claim that mood projections reflect genuine behavioral/semantic properties rather than shallow linguistic features.
